newsitem.title: UK: New ferry stability rules start to come into force.
newsitem.headline: New ferry stability rules start to come into force.

text.p: New ferry and passenger ship safety regulations resulting from the loss of the Estonia in 1994 became effective on Tuesday.

Amendments to the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), 1974, concentrate particularly on the stability of roll-on roll-off (ro-ro) ferries like the Estonia, which sank in the Baltic Sea with the loss of 852 lives.
The Estonia capsized when water flooded onto the vessel's cardeck after losing its bow loading visor.

But the stability requirements for existing vessels are being phased in so ships with 85 percent of a stability value set by the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) will not be required to comply fully until October 1, 1998.
Ships already reaching 97.5 percent of the A/Amax mathematical stability formula will be required to comply fully by October 1, 2005.

A new regulation has also been introduced for ro-ro passenger ships carrying more than 400 passengers, intended to ensure vessels can survive without capsizing if two compartments are flooded after damage.
IMO or classification societes, which will monitor much of the alterations, do not have figures indicating the number of vessels worlwide that need modification.
Regulations ensuring the watertight integrity of access doors have also been tightened by the new rules and provisions for liferafts and other lifesaving appliances beefed up.
Liferafts on passenger ships will be required to be self-righting or able to operate either way up, and at least one rescue vessel onboard will in future have to be a fast rescue boat.
Extra requirements for escape routes have also been introduced as have provisions for helicopter landing pads and improved communications systems.
